question: A team is setting up a Claude-assisted way of producing meeting notes. Nothing has been agreed or written down, people on the team hold different views about what the notes should contain, and the notes will be circulated to everyone who attended, so the team needs something it can depend on before this goes into regular use. Which sequence of steps is correct?
options: A) Run it over one week of real work; collect specific examples of where it fell short; draft the new way of working with the people who do the job; revise the written instructions and run it again.
B) Collect specific examples of where it fell short; draft the new way of working with the people who do the job; revise the written instructions and run it again; run it over one week of real work.
C) Revise the written instructions and run it again; run it over one week of real work; draft the new way of working with the people who do the job; collect specific examples of where it fell short.
D) Draft the new way of working with the people who do the job; run it over one week of real work; collect specific examples of where it fell short; revise the written instructions and run it again.
correct_answers: D) Draft the new way of working with the people who do the job; run it over one week of real work; collect specific examples of where it fell short; revise the written instructions and run it again.
explanations: Starting with a week of live use puts notes in front of every attendee while the team still disagrees about what those notes should contain, so the shortcomings it turns up describe several people's private habits rather than one shared way of working, and there is nothing agreed for the evidence to be measured against.

There is no agreed practice yet whose shortcomings could be collected, so the sequence opens with evidence it cannot have, and the week of real use lands at the very end, after the written instructions have already been revised, where the evidence it produces feeds nothing.
Nothing has been written down, so there are no instructions to revise first, and the specific failure examples are gathered last, at the point where there is no remaining step to act on them.

Correct. Drafting with the people who do the job settles the goal and how the work is split between them and Claude before anything is delegated, a week of real use then produces honest evidence against that agreed intent, specific failure examples say what to change, and revising the written instructions and running it again closes the evaluate-and-refine loop for another pass.
